**The Art of Wandering: In Praise of the Unproductive Mind**

There is a peculiar experiment that has haunted me since I first read about it. In 2014, a team of psychologists asked participants to sit alone in a bare room for six to fifteen minutes with no phone, no book, no writing material, no task. Just their thoughts. Before the session, some participants were given the option of administering mild electric shocks to themselves. They had all previously said they would pay money to avoid the shock. Yet when left alone with nothing but their own minds, a striking number—67 percent of men and 25 percent of women—chose to shock themselves rather than endure the quiet. Not because they were curious about the shock. Not because they enjoyed it. But because the prospect of unstructured inner time was so aversive that even a jolt of electricity seemed preferable.

I keep returning to this finding because it feels like a small, sharp diagnosis of a large cultural condition. We have built a world that is exquisitely designed to prevent us from ever being alone with our thoughts. We have filled every gap, every pause, every interval with input. The elevator ride, the queue, the red light, the commercial break, the walk from the car to the front door—all of it has been colonised by notifications, podcasts, music, audiobooks, headlines, messaging threads, and short videos. We speak with casual pride about being “busy” and with vague embarrassment about doing nothing. We have come to treat unstructured thought as a waste of time, or worse, as a small threat.

And yet, I want to argue, the capacity to wander mentally—to be unproductive, to drift, to follow a thought without a destination—is not a luxury or a vice. It is a necessary condition for creativity, emotional regulation, moral imagination, and even for a coherent sense of self. The loss of aimless thought may be one of the quiet crises of our age, less visible than political polarisation or economic inequality, but tangled up with both. To write freely, then, is not merely an exercise in filling pages. It is a small act of recovery: an attempt to reclaim the mind’s right to move without a purpose.

The modern attention economy did not emerge by accident. It is the result of vast engineering effort directed at a single goal: to capture and hold human awareness long enough to sell it to advertisers. Every infinite scroll, every autoplay, every red notification badge, every personalised feed is a refinement of that goal. The business model of the internet’s most successful companies depends on our inability to look away. They profit from our distraction. As the former design ethicist Tristan Harris has pointed out, when the product is free, the product is you. The result is an environment in which attention is perpetually harvested, and in which the user’s own intentions are often overridden by more powerful, better-funded intentions.

This would be troubling enough if attention were just another resource, like oil or timber. But attention is not one resource among many. Attention is the faculty by which we select what enters our conscious experience. It is the gatekeeper of the mind. To lose control of attention is to lose control of what we think, what we feel, what we remember, and ultimately who we become. William James, the father of American psychology, wrote in 1890 that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” If we do not choose what we attend to, someone else will choose for us. In an age of algorithmic feeds, that statement has become literal.

The cost of this is not just lost productivity, though we often frame it that way. The deeper cost is lost inner life. When every moment of silence is filled with stimulation, the mind never gets the chance to process its own material. It becomes a conduit for external inputs rather than a space for internal integration. The result is a paradox: we are more connected than ever, yet more scattered; more informed, yet less reflective; more available to others, yet less present to ourselves.

Neuroscience has begun to map what happens when the brain is not focused on an external task. In the 1990s, researchers using positron emission tomography noticed a set of brain regions that became more active when people were resting quietly, doing nothing in particular. This network—now called the default mode network—includes the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, angular gyrus, and hippocampus. It activates during mind-wandering, daydreaming, remembering the past, imagining the future, and thinking about other people’s mental states. The default mode network is not the absence of thought. It is a different kind of thought: associative, autobiographical, social, and imaginative.

When the brain is given unstructured time, it does not simply switch off. It begins to weave. It connects recent experiences to older memories. It rehearses conversations, replays mistakes, simulates possible futures. It generates the raw material for creative insight. Many people report that their best ideas arrive in the shower, on a walk, or just before sleep—precisely the moments when focused task attention is relaxed and the default mode network is free to do its integrative work. The mathematician Henri Poincaré famously described stepping onto a bus after a period of fruitless effort and suddenly seeing the solution to a problem he had been wrestling with for weeks. Insights like that are not accidents. They are the product of a mind given time to wander.

This is why the modern assault on boredom may be creatively costly. Boredom is not simply a negative state to be eliminated. It is a signal that the current situation is not supplying enough meaning or stimulation, and a prompt to search for new sources of interest. In moderate doses, boredom pushes us to read, to write, to draw, to explore, to invent games, to ask questions. It is the psychological equivalent of hunger: uncomfortable, but essential for survival. When we reflexively reach for our phones at the first twinge of boredom, we may be short-circuiting the very process that leads to original thought. We trade a moment of productive discomfort for a quick dose of external entertainment, and in doing so, we never learn to feed ourselves.

The writer Walter Benjamin once observed that boredom is “the dream bird that hatches the egg of experience.” He meant that the capacity to be bored—to tolerate a certain emptiness—is a condition for rich experience. In a society that treats boredom as an emergency to be solved immediately, we may be losing the ability to incubate experiences at all. We have become allergic to the pauses that make life intelligible.

Walking has long been the physical companion of wandering thought. The peripatetic philosophers of ancient Greece thought while pacing. Friedrich Nietzsche declared that “all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking.” William Wordsworth composed poetry on long rambles through the Lake District, often reciting aloud to the rhythm of his steps. Rebecca Solnit, in her book *Wanderlust: A History of Walking*, argues that walking is not merely a form of exercise but a mode of thinking. The steady, repetitive movement of the body seems to free the mind for associative movement. The pace of walking—about three miles an hour—is the pace of thought, of conversation, of attention to the world.

Yet many of us now walk with earbuds in, voices in our heads that are not our own. We walk while scrolling, while texting, while skimming news. We move through space without really being in space. The walk becomes another input delivery system rather than an opportunity for mental meandering. To reclaim the walk as a thinking practice, one must deliberately leave the phone at home, or at least silence it and keep it in a pocket. This is a small act with large consequences. It restores the connection between movement and reverie, between the body’s rhythm and the mind’s drift.

There is also a political dimension to all of this. A population that cannot pay attention is a population that cannot think clearly about complex problems. Democracy depends on citizens who can follow an argument, weigh evidence, hold conflicting ideas in mind, and resist the pull of simplistic narratives. But the attention economy trains us to do the opposite. It rewards outrage, brevity, novelty, and emotional intensity. It fragments our focus into ever smaller units. It makes sustained reflection feel difficult and even boring. In such an environment, the ability to concentrate becomes a form of resistance. The person who can sit with a long text, a difficult problem, or an uncomfortable ambiguity without reaching for a distraction is exercising a kind of civic virtue.

This is not a new concern. Long before smartphones, the philosopher Blaise Pascal wrote that “all of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.” He saw that humans seek ceaseless diversion because they cannot bear the truth of their own condition. We hunt, we gamble, we socialise, we build, we fight—all to avoid the silence that would force us to confront ourselves. The forms of diversion have changed, but the underlying pattern is the same. The smartphone is only the latest and most efficient machine for escaping the self.

Yet the self we are escaping may be exactly what we need. When we allow the mind to wander without external input, we encounter our own unfinished business. We remember what we have been avoiding. We feel feelings we have been too busy to feel. This is often uncomfortable, which is why we avoid it. But it is also necessary. Psychologists have found that people who engage in regular self-reflection tend to have better emotional regulation and more coherent life narratives. The unexamined life, as Socrates said, may not be worth living; but the overstimulated life may be equally impoverished. We need moments of unproductivity to let the psyche do its underground work.

There is a subtle difference between structured relaxation and true idleness. Many of us approach rest as another item on the to-do list: a meditation app, a yoga class, a wellness podcast, a “digital detox” retreat. These can be valuable, but they often import the logic of productivity into the very spaces meant to resist it. We optimise our rest, measure our sleep, track our steps, and curate our downtime. We feel guilty if a Sunday afternoon produces nothing we can point to. But the point of rest is not to improve future productivity. The point of rest is to be a human being rather than a human doing. The unproductive mind is not preparing for something else. It is already complete in its own meandering.

The artist Jenny Odell, in her book *How to Do Nothing*, argues that we need to reclaim attention as a form of love and care. She proposes that doing nothing is not about withdrawal but about reconnection—to our bodies, our places, our communities, and the natural world. The attention economy wants us to believe that value comes from constant self-promotion, endless networking, and maximal output. But Odell suggests a different economy of attention, one based on maintenance rather than growth, on noticing rather than producing, on being rather than appearing. In this economy, a long conversation with a friend, an afternoon watching birds, or a slow reading of a poem can be subversive acts.

I have felt this in my own life. On days when I give myself permission to be unproductive—to sit with a notebook and write whatever comes, to walk without a destination, to lie on the grass and watch clouds—I often feel a sense of spaciousness that no amount of efficient work can provide. Ideas arrive not as flashes but as slow currents. Emotions settle. The day acquires a texture that is not legible in a calendar or a to-do list. I remember that I am not a machine designed for output, but an organism designed for experience. This is not an escape from reality. It is a return to a thicker, more accurate reality.

What would it look like to build a life with more room for aimless thought? It would not require abandoning technology or retreating to a monastery. It would require small, repeated choices: leaving the phone outside the bedroom; taking a walk without headphones; sitting for ten minutes with a cup of tea and no agenda; writing three pages by hand before looking at any screen; allowing a commute to be silent; choosing one deep task over ten shallow ones. These choices are unglamorous and easily mocked. They do not produce measurable outcomes. But over time, they accumulate into a different kind of mind—one that is less reactive, more reflective, more capable of sustained attention and genuine curiosity.

One practical approach is to schedule idleness as seriously as work. This sounds paradoxical, but it works. If you wait until you have free time, the free time will never come. You must protect it. Put “do nothing” in the calendar. Guard it from intrusion. Tell others you are unavailable. Then, when the time comes, resist the urge to fill it with errands or entertainment. Sit. Stare. Drift. Let the mind go where it will. At first, it will feel uncomfortable—like an itch you are not allowed to scratch. That discomfort is the withdrawal symptom of an overstimulated mind. If you can endure it, it will pass, and something else will emerge: a thought, a memory, a feeling, a question. That emergence is the beginning of inner life.

There is also a role for technology itself in creating limits. The tools are not evil; the design is. We can use apps that block other apps, set timers, remove social media from our phones, or turn screens to grayscale. But the deeper change is not technological. It is cultural and psychological. We must decide that our attention is worth defending, that our inner life is worth cultivating, and that the unproductive mind is not an enemy but an ally. As long as we treat boredom as a problem to be solved by external stimulation, we will remain dependent on the very systems that fragment us. The moment we accept boredom as a gift, we begin to reclaim our minds.

I keep thinking about that experiment in the bare room. The participants who shocked themselves were not weak or unusual. They were simply human beings who had lost the capacity to tolerate their own company. They had been shaped by a culture that equates stillness with stagnation and distraction with vitality. But the fact that some people did not shock themselves—the fact that some could sit quietly for fifteen minutes and emerge not only intact but perhaps even refreshed—suggests another possibility. The capacity for solitude is not gone. It is dormant. It can be rebuilt. The question is whether we are willing to endure the initial discomfort, the itch of unproductivity, long enough to discover what lies beneath it.

In the end, writing freely is itself a form of wandering. It does not know where it is going. It follows a thread, loses it, finds another. It circles back. It contradicts itself. It is inefficient, meandering, unoptimized. And that is precisely its value. A text that is too tidy, too certain, too efficient in its argument may impress but it does not breathe. A wandering text, like a wandering mind, is alive. It opens spaces rather than closing them. It invites the reader to wander too. So perhaps this essay is not just about the unproductive mind; it is an example of it. It has no conclusion except the one you are about to draw. It has no destination except the next thought.

But that is not a failure. It is a small victory. For a few thousand words, I have allowed my mind to move without a purpose, and you have allowed yours to follow. In a world that demands constant output, that is a rare and necessary thing. The unproductive mind, it turns out, is not empty. It is full of the world—full of memory, imagination, possibility, and the quiet hum of a self that is still there, waiting to be heard. The task is not to silence the noise entirely; that may be impossible. The task is to make room, now and then, for the noise to recede, and to sit with whatever remains.

So the next time you find yourself with an empty moment, resist the urge to fill it. Let it stay empty. Watch what happens. You may feel restless, bored, even anxious. But you may also feel, after a while, a strange sense of spaciousness—a kind of permission to simply be. That spaciousness is not a waste. It is the soil in which thoughts grow. And in a world that is always shouting, the ability to sit in silence may be one of the most radical acts there is.

**The Art of Wandering: In Praise of the Unproductive Mind**

There is a peculiar experiment that has haunted me since I first read about it. In 2014, a team of psychologists asked participants to sit alone in a bare room for six to fifteen minutes with no phone, no book, no writing material, no task. Just their thoughts. Before the session, some participants were given the option of administering mild electric shocks to themselves. They had all previously said they would pay money to avoid the shock. Yet when left alone with nothing but their own minds, a striking number—67 percent of men and 25 percent of women—chose to shock themselves rather than endure the quiet. Not because they were curious about the shock. Not because they enjoyed it. But because the prospect of unstructured inner time was so aversive that even a jolt of electricity seemed preferable.

I keep returning to this finding because it feels like a small, sharp diagnosis of a large cultural condition. We have built a world that is exquisitely designed to prevent us from ever being alone with our thoughts. We have filled every gap, every pause, every interval with input. The elevator ride, the queue, the red light, the commercial break, the walk from the car to the front door—all of it has been colonised by notifications, podcasts, music, audiobooks, headlines, messaging threads, and short videos. We speak with casual pride about being "busy" and with vague embarrassment about doing nothing. We have come to treat unstructured thought as a waste of time, or worse, as a small threat.

And yet, I want to argue, the capacity to wander mentally—to be unproductive, to drift, to follow a thought without a destination—is not a luxury or a vice. It is a necessary condition for creativity, emotional regulation, moral imagination, and even for a coherent sense of self. The loss of aimless thought may be one of the quiet crises of our age, less visible than political polarisation or economic inequality, but tangled up with both. To write freely, then, is not merely an exercise in filling pages. It is a small act of recovery: an attempt to reclaim the mind's right to move without a purpose.

The modern attention economy did not emerge by accident. It is the result of vast engineering effort directed at a single goal: to capture and hold human awareness long enough to sell it to advertisers. Every infinite scroll, every autoplay, every red notification badge, every personalised feed is a refinement of that goal. The business model of the internet's most successful companies depends on our inability to look away. They profit from our distraction. As the former design ethicist Tristan Harris has pointed out, when the product is free, the product is you. The result is an environment in which attention is perpetually harvested, and in which the user's own intentions are often overridden by more powerful, better-funded intentions.

This would be troubling enough if attention were just another resource, like oil or timber. But attention is not one resource among many. Attention is the faculty by which we select what enters our conscious experience. It is the gatekeeper of the mind. To lose control of attention is to lose control of what we think, what we feel, what we remember, and ultimately who we become. William James, the father of American psychology, wrote in 1890 that "my experience is what I agree to attend to." If we do not choose what we attend to, someone else will choose for us. In an age of algorithmic feeds, that statement has become literal.

The cost of this is not just lost productivity, though we often frame it that way. The deeper cost is lost inner life. When every moment of silence is filled with stimulation, the mind never gets the chance to process its own material. It becomes a conduit for external inputs rather than a space for internal integration. The result is a paradox: we are more connected than ever, yet more scattered; more informed, yet less reflective; more available to others, yet less present to ourselves.

Neuroscience has begun to map what happens when the brain is not focused on an external task. In the 1990s, researchers using positron emission tomography noticed a set of brain regions that became more active when people were resting quietly, doing nothing in particular. This network—now called the default mode network—includes the medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, angular gyrus, and hippocampus. It activates during mind-wandering, daydreaming, remembering the past, imagining the future, and thinking about other people's mental states. The default mode network is not the absence of thought. It is a different kind of thought: associative, autobiographical, social, and imaginative.

When the brain is given unstructured time, it does not simply switch off. It begins to weave. It connects recent experiences to older memories. It rehearses conversations, replays mistakes, simulates possible futures. It generates the raw material for creative insight. Many people report that their best ideas arrive in the shower, on a walk, or just before sleep—precisely the moments when focused task attention is relaxed and the default mode network is free to do its integrative work. The mathematician Henri Poincaré famously described stepping onto a bus after a period of fruitless effort and suddenly seeing the solution to a problem he had been wrestling with for weeks. Insights like that are not accidents. They are the product of a mind given time to wander.

This is why the modern assault on boredom may be creatively costly. Boredom is not simply a negative state to be eliminated. It is a signal that the current situation is not supplying enough meaning or stimulation, and a prompt to search for new sources of interest. In moderate doses, boredom pushes us to read, to write, to draw, to explore, to invent games, to ask questions. It is the psychological equivalent of hunger: uncomfortable, but essential for survival. When we reflexively reach for our phones at the first twinge of boredom, we may be short-circuiting the very process that leads to original thought. We trade a moment of productive discomfort for a quick dose of external entertainment, and in doing so, we never learn to feed ourselves.

The writer Walter Benjamin once observed that boredom is "the dream bird that hatches the egg of experience." He meant that the capacity to be bored—to tolerate a certain emptiness—is a condition for rich experience. In a society that treats boredom as an emergency to be solved immediately, we may be losing the ability to incubate experiences at all. We have become allergic to the pauses that make life intelligible.

Walking has long been the physical companion of wandering thought. The peripatetic philosophers of ancient Greece thought while pacing. Friedrich Nietzsche declared that "all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking." William Wordsworth composed poetry on long rambles through the Lake District, often reciting aloud to the rhythm of his steps. Rebecca Solnit, in her book *Wanderlust: A History of Walking*, argues that walking is not merely a form of exercise but a mode of thinking. The steady, repetitive movement of the body seems to free the mind for associative movement. The pace of walking—about three miles an hour—is the pace of thought, of conversation, of attention to the world.

Yet many of us now walk with earbuds in, voices in our heads that are not our own. We walk while scrolling, while texting, while skimming news. We move through space without really being in space. The walk becomes another input delivery system rather than an opportunity for mental meandering. To reclaim the walk as a thinking practice, one must deliberately leave the phone at home, or at least silence it and keep it in a pocket. This is a small act with large consequences. It restores the connection between movement and reverie, between the body's rhythm and the mind's drift.

There is also a political dimension to all of this. A population that cannot pay attention is a population that cannot think clearly about complex problems. Democracy depends on citizens who can follow an argument, weigh evidence, hold conflicting ideas in mind, and resist the pull of simplistic narratives. But the attention economy trains us to do the opposite. It rewards outrage, brevity, novelty, and emotional intensity. It fragments our focus into ever smaller units. It makes sustained reflection feel difficult and even boring. In such an environment, the ability to concentrate becomes a form of resistance. The person who can sit with a long text, a difficult problem, or an uncomfortable ambiguity without reaching for a distraction is exercising a kind of civic virtue.

This is not a new concern. Long before smartphones, the philosopher Blaise Pascal wrote that "all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone." He saw that humans seek ceaseless diversion because they cannot bear the truth of their own condition. We hunt, we gamble, we socialise, we build, we fight—all to avoid the silence that would force us to confront ourselves. The forms of diversion have changed, but the underlying pattern is the same. The smartphone is only the latest and most efficient machine for escaping the self.

Yet the self we are escaping may be exactly what we need. When we allow the mind to wander without external input, we encounter our own unfinished business. We remember what we have been avoiding. We feel feelings we have been too busy to feel. This is often uncomfortable, which is why we avoid it. But it is also necessary. Psychologists have found that people who engage in regular self-reflection tend to have better emotional regulation and more coherent life narratives. The unexamined life, as Socrates said, may not be worth living; but the overstimulated life may be equally impoverished. We need moments of unproductivity to let the psyche do its underground work.

There is a subtle difference between structured relaxation and true idleness. Many of us approach rest as another item on the to-do list: a meditation app, a yoga class, a wellness podcast, a "digital detox" retreat. These can be valuable, but they often import the logic of productivity into the very spaces meant to resist it. We optimise our rest, measure our sleep, track our steps, and curate our downtime. We feel guilty if a Sunday afternoon produces nothing we can point to. But the point of rest is not to improve future productivity. The point of rest is to be a human being rather than a human doing. The unproductive mind is not preparing for something else. It is already complete in its own meandering.

The artist Jenny Odell, in her book *How to Do Nothing*, argues that we need to reclaim attention as a form of love and care. She proposes that doing nothing is not about withdrawal but about reconnection—to our bodies, our places, our communities, and the natural world. The attention economy wants us to believe that value comes from constant self-promotion, endless networking, and maximal output. But Odell suggests a different economy of attention, one based on maintenance rather than growth, on noticing rather than producing, on being rather than appearing. In this economy, a long conversation with a friend, an afternoon watching birds, or a slow reading of a poem can be subversive acts.

I have felt this in my own life. On days when I give myself permission to be unproductive—to sit with a notebook and write whatever comes, to walk without a destination, to lie on the grass and watch clouds—I often feel a sense of spaciousness that no amount of efficient work can provide. Ideas arrive not as flashes but as slow currents. Emotions settle. The day acquires a texture that is not legible in a calendar or a to-do list. I remember that I am not a machine designed for output, but an organism designed for experience. This is not an escape from reality. It is a return to a thicker, more accurate reality.

What would it look like to build a life with more room for aimless thought? It would not require abandoning technology or retreating to a monastery. It would require small, repeated choices: leaving the phone outside the bedroom; taking a walk without headphones; sitting for ten minutes with a cup of tea and no agenda; writing three pages by hand before looking at any screen; allowing a commute to be silent; choosing one deep task over ten shallow ones. These choices are unglamorous and easily mocked. They do not produce measurable outcomes. But over time, they accumulate into a different kind of mind—one that is less reactive, more reflective, more capable of sustained attention and genuine curiosity.

One practical approach is to schedule idleness as seriously as work. This sounds paradoxical, but it works. If you wait until you have free time, the free time will never come. You must protect it. Put "do nothing" in the calendar. Guard it from intrusion. Tell others you are unavailable. Then, when the time comes, resist the urge to fill it with errands or entertainment. Sit. Stare. Drift. Let the mind go where it will. At first, it will feel uncomfortable—like an itch you are not allowed to scratch. That discomfort is the withdrawal symptom of an overstimulated mind. If you can endure it, it will pass, and something else will emerge: a thought, a memory, a feeling, a question. That emergence is the beginning of inner life.

There is also a role for technology itself in creating limits. The tools are not evil; the design is. We can use apps that block other apps, set timers, remove social media from our phones, or turn screens to grayscale. But the deeper change is not technological. It is cultural and psychological. We must decide that our attention is worth defending, that our inner life is worth cultivating, and that the unproductive mind is not an enemy but an ally. As long as we treat boredom as a problem to be solved by external stimulation, we will remain dependent on the very systems that fragment us. The moment we accept boredom as a gift, we begin to reclaim our minds.

I keep thinking about that experiment in the bare room. The participants who shocked themselves were not weak or unusual. They were simply human beings who had lost the capacity to tolerate their own company. They had been shaped by a culture that equates stillness with stagnation and distraction with vitality. But the fact that some people did not shock themselves—the fact that some could sit quietly for fifteen minutes and emerge not only intact but perhaps even refreshed—suggests another possibility. The capacity for solitude is not gone. It is dormant. It can be rebuilt. The question is whether we are willing to endure the initial discomfort, the itch of unproductivity, long enough to discover what lies beneath it.

In the end, writing freely is itself a form of wandering. It does not know where it is going. It follows a thread, loses it, finds another. It circles back. It contradicts itself. It is inefficient, meandering, unoptimized. And that is precisely its value. A text that is too tidy, too certain, too efficient in its argument may impress but it does not breathe. A wandering text, like a wandering mind, is alive. It opens spaces rather than closing them. It invites the reader to wander too. So perhaps this essay is not just about the unproductive mind; it is an example of it. It has no conclusion except the one you are about to draw. It has no destination except the next thought.

But that is not a failure. It is a small victory. For a few thousand words, I have allowed my mind to move without a purpose, and you have allowed yours to follow. In a world that demands constant output, that is a rare and necessary thing. The unproductive mind, it turns out, is not empty. It is full of the world—full of memory, imagination, possibility, and the quiet hum of a self that is still there, waiting to be heard. The task is not to silence the noise entirely; that may be impossible. The task is to make room, now and then, for the noise to recede, and to sit with whatever remains.

So the next time you find yourself with an empty moment, resist the urge to fill it. Let it stay empty. Watch what happens. You may feel restless, bored, even anxious. But you may also feel, after a while, a strange sense of spaciousness—a kind of permission to simply be. That spaciousness is not a waste. It is the soil in which thoughts grow. And in a world that is always shouting, the ability to sit in silence may be one of the most radical acts there is.
